blocks.content: This new module turns to HTTP, the protocol that makes the actual web itself work. Everything covered so far in this course, packets, TCP, IP addresses, DNS, was about getting data from one place to another reliably. HTTP is the actual conversation that happens once that connection exists, the language a browser and a server actually speak to each other.

If you have ever loaded a webpage, used an app, or called an API, you have used HTTP, almost certainly without ever thinking about it directly. This opening topic builds the foundational mental model everything else in this module rests on.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437678363-311181330.png
1. HTTP Sits on Top of a Reliable Connection
blocks.text: 1. HTTP Sits on Top of a Reliable Connection

blocks.content: HTTP does not handle its own reliability, ordering, or connection setup at all, it relies entirely on TCP, covered in full in the Transport Layer and TCP Deep Dive modules, to actually deliver its messages correctly. HTTP is genuinely just the language spoken once that reliable connection already exists underneath it.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437678364-292164147.png
blocks.alt: HTTP Sits on Top of a Reliable Connection

blocks.title: A direct callback to the transport layer
blocks.content: Every reliability guarantee covered in the reliability-in-tcp topic, ordered delivery, resending lost data, is silently working underneath every single HTTP exchange, HTTP itself never has to think about any of it.
2. The Core Model: Request and Response
blocks.text: 2. The Core Model: Request and Response

blocks.content: HTTP follows an extremely simple, strict pattern: the client always asks first, sending a request, and the server always answers, sending a response back. This direction never reverses, a server never spontaneously initiates contact with a client on its own using plain HTTP.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437678364-105463281.png
blocks.alt: The Core Model: Request and Response

blocks.content: 3. HTTP Is Stateless By Default

This is a genuinely important, foundational property worth understanding early. Each individual HTTP request is treated completely independently by the server, with no automatic, built in memory connecting it to any earlier request, even one from the exact same client just moments before.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437678365-577207537.png

blocks.title: Why this matters, forward pointer
blocks.content: This statelessness is exactly why cookies and sessions, both covered in their own dedicated topics later in this module, had to be invented, to let a website actually remember who you are across multiple separate requests despite HTTP itself having no built in memory at all.
4. What an HTTP Request Actually Contains
blocks.text: 4. What an HTTP Request Actually Contains

blocks.content: A request has a method, describing what action the client wants performed, forward pointer to the dedicated http-methods topic, a path, identifying exactly which resource on the server it wants, headers, carrying various pieces of metadata about the request, and an optional body, carrying actual data being sent, like a form submission.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437678365-102098772.png
blocks.alt: What an HTTP Request Actually Contains

blocks.content: 5. What an HTTP Response Actually Contains
blocks.text: 5. What an HTTP Response Actually Contains

blocks.content: A response mirrors this structure. It has a status code, a specific number telling the client exactly what happened, forward pointer to the dedicated status-codes topic, headers, carrying metadata about the response, and an optional body, carrying the actual content being returned, an HTML page, a JSON payload, an image, whatever was actually requested.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437678765-312854988.png
blocks.alt: What an HTTP Response Actually Contains

6. A Real World Analogy

A restaurant captures this well. A customer places an order, the request, describing exactly what they want. The kitchen prepares it. The waiter brings the finished dish back to the table, the response. The customer never walks into the kitchen and starts cooking themselves, and the kitchen never sends food out to a table that never actually ordered anything.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437678765-133742023.png
7. HTTP Is Genuinely Everywhere

Loading any webpage at all uses HTTP. Calling an API uses HTTP. Nearly every modern application talking to a server, whether it is a mobile app, a desktop program, or a website, is built on HTTP underneath, even when the actual user interface looks nothing like a traditional webpage at all.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437678783-378013977.png

8. Common Mistakes and Key Takeaways

["Assuming a server can spontaneously push data to a client using plain HTTP, when the client always has to initiate every single exchange first.","Assuming HTTP itself remembers who you are between requests, when it is genuinely stateless by default, that memory has to be built on top using cookies and sessions.","HTTP is the language spoken over an already reliable TCP connection, not a replacement for TCP itself.","The client always sends the request first; the server only ever responds.","Every HTTP request has a method, a path, headers, and an optional body.","Every HTTP response has a status code, headers, and an optional body."]
items: Assuming a server can spontaneously push data to a client using plain HTTP, when the client always has to initiate every single exchange first.
Assuming HTTP itself remembers who you are between requests, when it is genuinely stateless by default, that memory has to be built on top using cookies and sessions.
HTTP is the language spoken over an already reliable TCP connection, not a replacement for TCP itself.
The client always sends the request first; the server only ever responds.
Every HTTP request has a method, a path, headers, and an optional body.
Every HTTP response has a status code, headers, and an optional body.
